section.title: Woe to Ariel
section.sectionRationale: Continuing the woes, chapters 28 to 33, this oracle turns to Jerusalem herself, called Ariel, besieged by the LORD and yet suddenly delivered from her attackers. It exposes worship that is mere lip service, a sealed scroll no one can read, and a people who hide their plans from God as if He, the potter, could be deceived by His own clay.
section.thesis: The LORD besieges Ariel, His own city, exposing worship that honors Him with lips while hearts stay far away, yet He will suddenly deliver her from her attackers, unseal the scroll, open deaf ears and blind eyes, and bring the humble to rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the siege of Ariel and her sudden deliverance from the nations; the sealed scroll and worship that is mere lip service; woe to those who hide their plans from the LORD, the potter mistaken for clay; and the promised day when the deaf hear, the blind see, and the humble rejoice.

units.label: The siege of Ariel and her sudden deliverance
units.note: besieged, then rescued like waking from a dream

verses.text: Woe to you, O {{ariel|Ariel}}, the city of Ariel where David camped! Year upon year let your festivals recur.
And I will constrain Ariel, and there will be mourning and lamentation; she will be like an altar hearth before Me.
I will camp in a circle around you; I will besiege you with towers and set up siege works against you.
You will be brought low, you will speak from the ground, and out of the dust your words will be muffled. Your voice will be like a spirit from the ground; your speech will whisper out of the dust.
But your many foes will be like fine dust, the multitude of the ruthless like blowing chaff. Then suddenly, in an instant,
you will be visited by the LORD of Hosts with thunder and earthquake and loud noise, with windstorm and tempest and consuming flame of fire.
All the many nations going out to battle against Ariel, even all who war against her, laying siege and attacking her, will be like a dream, like a vision in the night,

as when a hungry man dreams he is eating, then awakens still hungry; as when a thirsty man dreams he is drinking, then awakens faint and parched. So will it be for all the many nations who go to battle against Mount Zion.

units.label: The sealed scroll, worship as lip service

verses.text: Stop and be astonished; blind yourselves and be sightless; be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not from strong drink.
For the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep. He has shut your eyes, O prophets; He has covered your heads, O seers.
And the entire vision will be to you like the words {{chatam|sealed}} in a scroll. If it is handed to someone to read, he will say, “I cannot, because it is sealed.”
Or if the scroll is handed to one unable to read, he will say, “I cannot read.”
Therefore the Lord said: “These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men.
Therefore I will again confound these people with wonder upon wonder. The wisdom of the wise will vanish, and the intelligence of the intelligent will be hidden.”

units.label: Woe to those who hide from the LORD

verses.text: Woe to those who dig deep to hide their plans from the LORD. In darkness they do their works and say, “Who sees us, and who will know?”

You have turned things upside down, as if the potter were regarded as clay. Shall what is formed say to him who formed it, “He did not make me”? Can the pottery say of the potter, “He has no understanding”?
In a very short time, will not Lebanon become an orchard, and the orchard seem like a forest?

units.label: The deaf hear, the blind see, the humble rejoice

verses.text: On that day the deaf will hear the words of the scroll, and out of the deep darkness the eyes of the blind will see.
The humble will increase their joy in the LORD, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.
For the ruthless will vanish, the mockers will disappear, and all who look for evil will be cut down,
those who indict a man with a word, who ensnare the mediator at the gate, and who with false charges deprive the innocent of justice.
Therefore the LORD who redeemed Abraham says of the house of Jacob: “No longer will Jacob be ashamed and no more will his face grow pale.
For when he sees his children around him, the work of My hands, they will honor My name, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and they will stand in awe of the God of Israel.
Then the wayward in spirit will come to understanding, and those who grumble will accept instruction.”

ariel.gloss: A name for Jerusalem meaning altar hearth, or possibly lion of God, playing on the fire that consumes sacrifices on the altar. Naming the besieged city Ariel casts the coming siege itself as a strange kind of offering, the city itself becoming like an altar hearth before the LORD.

chatam.gloss: To seal, to close up so the contents cannot be read or accessed until properly opened. The vision sealed like a scroll no one can read pictures spiritual blindness so complete that God's own revelation becomes unintelligible, an image Revelation later reverses when only the Lamb is found worthy to open the sealed scroll, Revelation 5.

basic.context: Jerusalem, called Ariel, faces a siege so severe that she is compared to a voice whispering from the dust, yet the LORD suddenly and dramatically delivers her, so that her many attackers vanish like a dream upon waking. At the same time, the LORD exposes worship that is mere lip service, a sealed scroll that no one can read, and rulers who scheme in secret as if the potter could not see His own clay.
basic.hermeneutics: The siege and sudden deliverance of Ariel most plausibly describes the historical rescue of Jerusalem from Sennacherib's Assyrian siege in 701 BC, when the city was miraculously spared, 2 Kings 19:35-36. The sealed scroll and hollow worship expose a real, ongoing spiritual condition, hearts far from God despite outward religion, which Jesus later quotes directly of the religious leaders of His own day, Matthew 15:8-9.
basic.originalLanguages: Jerusalem is called Ariel, likely altar hearth, casting the coming siege as a strange offering upon the city itself. The prophetic vision becomes chatham, sealed, entirely inaccessible to a people who can neither read nor comprehend it, the very image Revelation later reverses when the Lamb alone proves worthy to break the seals and open the scroll, Revelation 5:1-9.
basic.typology: The sealed scroll that no one can open or read anticipates the scroll in Revelation 5, sealed until the Lamb, Christ, alone is found worthy to open it. The promised day when the deaf hear and the blind see anticipates and is directly fulfilled in Christ's own healing ministry, cited by Jesus Himself as proof of His messianic identity, Matthew 11:4-5.
basic.christ: Jesus quotes verse 13 directly against the Pharisees, these people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me, Matthew 15:8-9, exposing the same hollow religion centuries later. His healing ministry, opening deaf ears and blind eyes, Matthew 11:4-5, Luke 4:18, directly fulfills verse 18's promise, and He alone, the Lamb once slain, is found worthy to open the sealed scroll that no human being could open, Revelation 5:1-9.
basic.god: God sees straight through outward religious performance to the state of the heart, and He is not fooled by those who plot in secret, since the potter always knows His own clay. Yet even His exposure of hollow worship and secret scheming serves a redemptive purpose: to bring about the day when the deaf hear, the blind see, and the humble rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 19:35-36 records the historical, sudden deliverance of Jerusalem from Sennacherib's siege. Matthew 15:8-9 quotes Isaiah 29:13 directly against religious leaders whose worship is mere lip service. Matthew 11:4-5 records Jesus citing the healing of the deaf and blind as proof of His messianic identity. Revelation 5:1-9 pictures Christ, the Lamb, alone worthy to open the sealed scroll.
basic.oneStory: This chapter moves from a besieged, humbled city suddenly and miraculously delivered, through an exposure of empty religious performance, to the promised day when the deaf hear, the blind see, and the humble rejoice in God. Christ fulfills every strand: He quotes this chapter against hollow worship, heals the deaf and blind as this chapter foretold, and alone is worthy to unseal the scroll no human hand could open.

context.literary:
The chapter is built on a tight pattern of reversal. Verses 1 to 8 move from siege to rescue, with the hinge in verse 5, 'Then suddenly, in an instant,' and an enemy that dissolves like a dream. Verses 9 to 14 then turn the camera on Jerusalem's own people, who are told to stagger and be blind. Verses 15 and 16 pronounce a woe, the formal marker that has run through chapters 28 to 33, on those who think their plans can be hidden. Verses 17 to 24 close with a string of 'on that day' reversals. The scroll that no one could read in verses 11 and 12 is read by the deaf in verse 18, the blind see, the humble rejoice, and the wayward finally learn.

The opening is written as a double meaning. Verse 1 says 'Year upon year let your festivals recur,' which sounds like a blessing on the calendar of worship, but it is spoken inside a woe. The altar fires keep burning, and in verse 2 the city itself becomes the thing laid on the hearth. The poet then speaks in the voice of the besieged: the city whispers from the dust, verse 4, like a voice from a grave.

The central diagnosis in verse 13 is introduced by 'Therefore the Lord said,' and its twin appears at verse 14, 'Therefore I will again confound these people.' The pairing matters. Their lips are near and their hearts are far, so God answers with wonder that leaves the learned bewildered. The vocabulary of teaching keeps returning, 'rules taught by men' in verse 13 and 'accept instruction' in verse 24, so that the whole chapter frames the question of who teaches God's people and what they are able to receive.
context.historical:
Ariel here is Jerusalem, the city David took, 2 Samuel 5:7, and the language of verses 1 to 8 fits the crisis of 701 BC, when the Assyrian king Sennacherib overran Judah and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem, 2 Kings 18:13 and 19:35-36. Judah's own officials had been busy with diplomacy, and the chapters around this one, 28 to 31, show them courting Egypt in secret. Verse 15, 'dig deep to hide their plans,' catches that mood. Plans were being laid in the dark rooms of the palace while Isaiah was standing in the open with a word from the LORD.

The religious scene was not empty. Hezekiah had cleared out much of the high place worship, 2 Kings 18:4, and the temple in Jerusalem had its festivals and its sacrifices, so the charge in verse 13 is not that Judah has abandoned worship. It is that worship has become habit, learned by rote and kept going alongside political schemes that never asked what God thought.

The prophets and seers of verse 10 were the people whose office was to see for the nation. In a court that wanted good news, their vision had become something nobody could or would read. Isaiah elsewhere speaks of sealing up the teaching among his disciples, Isaiah 8:16, which suggests the image of a closed scroll would have felt familiar to the first readers. A written document in that world was literally sealed with clay or wax and a stamp, and only someone with authority could break it.

The hearers also knew what a siege felt like. Jerusalem lived by its water and its walls, and when the Assyrian army camped around it the voice from the dust would not have been a metaphor. It was what a city sounded like when it was starving and afraid.
context.canonical:
Isaiah 29 is quoted and echoed more widely than its length suggests. Jesus takes verse 13 and turns it on the scribes and Pharisees, Matthew 15:8-9 and Mark 7:6-7. Both Gospels follow the Greek version of Isaiah, which reads 'in vain do they worship Me, teaching as doctrines the precepts of men,' as the BSB footnote shows. Paul takes verse 14 as the shape of the cross, God destroying the wisdom of the wise, 1 Corinthians 1:19. He uses the potter and clay imagery of verse 16 when he answers the question of God's justice, Romans 9:20-21, and he borrows the 'spirit of stupor' language of verse 10, with Deuteronomy 29:4, when he asks why many in Israel did not see, Romans 11:8.

The image of the sealed scroll connects forward to Daniel 12:4, where words are shut up and sealed until the time of the end, and to Revelation 5:1-5, where a scroll sealed with seven seals can be opened only by the Lion of Judah, the Lamb.

The promise of verse 17, that Lebanon will become an orchard and the orchard will seem like a forest, comes back in nearly the same words in Isaiah 32:15, where it is tied to the Spirit being poured out. The sudden rescue of verse 7 and following has parallels in Psalm 73:20, which pictures the wicked as a dream when one wakes. The hope for a final siege of Jerusalem undone by the LORD is carried forward in Zechariah 12:9. And the hope of verse 18 for the deaf and the blind is picked up in Isaiah 35:5, then in Isaiah 42:7, and finally in Luke 4:18 and Matthew 11:5.

So the chapter sits at a crossing point. It looks back to Sinai-shaped worship and forward to a Teacher who opens ears.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted a nervous, clever, religiously busy people to see that their situation had been misread from the inside. The danger was not the army outside the walls, because that army would be dealt with by the LORD in an instant, verses 5 to 8. The danger was the condition within: a people who could recite the forms but whose hearts were elsewhere, who could hold a vision in their hands and not read it, who thought that plans made in secret were invisible to the one who made them.

He also meant to give hope that is larger than rescue. The chapter ends not at the lifting of the siege but at a changed people. The deaf hear words, the blind see, the humble rejoice, and the grumblers learn. Isaiah's first hearers were meant to leave the chapter humbled and expectant at once. They were to stop trusting their wisdom, because the LORD would wreck it in verse 14, and to wait for the day when God Himself would give the understanding they could not produce.

The woe of verses 15 and 16 gives the pastoral edge. To plot against God's counsel is to invert the order of things, as though the pot instructed the potter. Isaiah wants the courtiers to hear how absurd that sounds.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The siege and the dream-like fading of the nations in verses 1 to 8 are a description of one particular event and one particular promise. They are not a formula guaranteeing that every besieged city will be rescued. Believers have suffered sieges, and God's people have been carried off, so the verses must not be pressed into a guarantee about any given war.

What is prescriptive is the diagnosis of worship in verse 13. Lips that draw near while hearts stay far, and instruction received as human tradition rather than as God's word, are always possible, and Jesus applies the verse to His own day. The chapter therefore tests every pattern of religious life: not whether we have forms, which Scripture does not forbid, but whether the forms are in the service of a living relationship.

The vision of verses 17 to 24 is likewise promise rather than command. It cannot be produced by effort, which is the point. The believer receives eyes and ears from God, and then, as the chapter ends, learns and walks in them.

debates.question: Who causes the scroll to be sealed and understanding to fail in verses 9 to 12, God Himself or the people's own hardened refusal?

views.label: God actively seals understanding as a judicial act
views.case: Verse 10 states plainly that the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep and shut your eyes, suggesting an active, judicial hardening in response to persistent unfaithfulness, similar to Isaiah 6:9-10. Paul reads it this way in Romans 11:8, where the spirit of stupor is something God gave.

views.label: The people's own hollow worship and refusal to listen brings this blindness on themselves
views.case: Verse 13's diagnosis, they honor Me with their lips but their hearts are far from Me, suggests the sealing described is the natural, deserved consequence of choosing empty ritual over genuine devotion, with God's judicial action confirming rather than initiating their self-chosen blindness.

debates.bearing: Scripture elsewhere holds both truths together without contradiction: God's judicial hardening of persistently unfaithful hearts, Isaiah 6:9-10, Romans 1:24-28, is not arbitrary but a response to prior human rejection of the truth, so both readings describe the same reality from different angles.

debates.question: Does the rescue of Ariel in verses 5 to 8 describe 701 BC, or a final siege at the end of the age?

views.label: The deliverance from Sennacherib
views.case: The setting of the surrounding chapters is the Assyrian crisis, and the story of the angel striking down the Assyrian camp overnight, 2 Kings 19:35 and Isaiah 37:36, fits the image of a great army gone when the people woke. The thunder, earthquake and fire of verse 6 are the usual language of the LORD's coming to fight for His people.

views.label: A final siege of Jerusalem
views.case: The language of 'all the many nations' in verses 7 and 8 is wider than one Assyrian army, and Zechariah 12:9 speaks of the LORD destroying all the nations that come against Jerusalem. On this reading the chapter looks past 701 to a last gathering of the nations.

views.label: A pattern that is realized more than once
views.case: Isaiah regularly speaks in a way that fits a near event and gives it a larger shape. The nations as a dream pattern describes how the LORD deals with every power that sets itself against Zion, and Sennacherib is its first great example.

debates.bearing: The Sennacherib setting gives the passage its ground in history, while the wide language of 'many nations' lets later readers see in it a pattern of how God treats the enemies of His people. Neither reading removes the main point, that the rescue comes from the LORD alone.

study.originalLanguages:
The name Ariel is probably built on the word for a hearth or altar top, which is how the BSB footnote gives it, 'Altar Hearth,' with Lion of God as the alternative. The ambiguity is useful. Jerusalem is a lion in her self-image and an altar hearth in the LORD's. In verse 2 the city is 'like an altar hearth before Me,' a place where something is burned. The one who thought of himself as the hunter is the offering. The name is used five times in these first verses, so that it rings like a bell.

The word for the 'spirit from the ground' in verse 4 is ob, the word used elsewhere for a medium or the spirit of the dead that a medium summons, Isaiah 8:19 and 1 Samuel 28:7-8. Jerusalem, the city that should be speaking God's word with authority, will whisper from the dust like a ghost. The image is a humiliation: the voice of God's city will sound like the voice of the dead.

The 'deep sleep' in verse 10 is tardemah, the word used of the sleep God caused to fall on Adam, Genesis 2:21, and on Saul's whole camp when David walked through it, 1 Samuel 26:12. It is a sleep from which one cannot be woken by ordinary means. In Genesis it is the sleep of creative surgery, in Samuel the sleep of helpless vulnerability, and here it is the sleep of judgment on those who ought to be the nation's watchmen.

The key word in verse 13 is the phrase translated 'rules taught by men.' The Hebrew phrase is a commandment of men, and the participle behind 'taught' carries the sense of something learned and repeated. It describes worship that has become a memorised routine. The Greek Old Testament softens the wording to 'teaching as doctrines the precepts of men,' and Matthew and Mark follow the Greek, so Jesus' quotation and Isaiah's Hebrew say the same thing in slightly different language, a point the BSB footnote records.

In verse 14 the God who will 'again confound' uses a word for wonder, pele, a root usually reserved for His mighty acts, such as the exodus. Here the same word is the instrument of confusion. His wonders are so far beyond human wisdom that the wise cannot follow them.

In verse 16 the people have 'turned things upside down,' from a root that means overturn, the word used of the overthrow of Sodom in Genesis 19:25. The inversion is moral and cosmic: the pot is putting itself in the potter's seat. And in verse 19 the 'humble' and 'poor' are the two words, anavim and evyonim, that Israel's worship uses of those who have no standing except in the LORD.

typology.type: Ariel as the hearth where the city itself is laid, Isaiah 29:2
typology.fulfillment: The city is told it will be 'like an altar hearth before Me,' a place of burning that the LORD Himself prepares. The type is real only in a limited sense, since it describes judgment on a people and not an atoning offering. Yet the New Testament uses the language of the altar and the city together when it says that Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through His own blood, Hebrews 13:11-12. Where Ariel burns because of her failure, Christ is offered because of His love. The escalation is that the Offering is not the city but its Lord, and the fire that should have fallen on His people falls on Him.

typology.type: The sealed scroll that cannot be read, Isaiah 29:11-12
typology.fulfillment: The vision becomes a closed document, and neither the learned nor the unlearned can open it. Revelation 5:1-5 takes up the picture: a scroll sealed with seven seals that no one in heaven or on earth can open, until the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Lamb who was slain, is found worthy. Luke records the same pattern on the road to Emmaus, where Jesus opened the Scriptures to two disciples who could not read them, Luke 24:27 and 24:45. The type falls short in that Isaiah's scroll is sealed in judgment and Revelation's is sealed until the right Person arrives.

typology.type: The deaf who hear the words of the scroll and the blind who see, Isaiah 29:18
typology.fulfillment: The promised reversal of verse 18 is taken up by Jesus when John the Baptist's disciples ask if He is the coming One. He answers with the signs of the blind receiving sight and the deaf hearing, Matthew 11:4-5, and He announces Isaiah 61:1 in the synagogue at Nazareth, Luke 4:18. Mark records a deaf man healed with the cry that Jesus has made the deaf hear and the mute speak, Mark 7:37. The correspondence is literal and spiritual at once. The type is surpassed because physical healing is a sign of the larger gift, the opening of minds to understand the word, Luke 24:45.

typology.type: The potter and the clay, Isaiah 29:16
typology.fulfillment: The inversion of verse 16 sits alongside Isaiah 45:9 and 64:8 in a long line of potter and clay language. Paul draws on verse 16 to answer the person who questions God's justice, Romans 9:20-21. The correspondence is that the Creator has the right to shape His creatures, and the escalation is in Christ, the One through whom all things were made, Colossians 1:16. The type has limits: God is a Potter who also becomes clay, entering the human condition in Jesus, so that the one who shapes also shares.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most plainly by quotation. Jesus takes verse 13 and makes it a mirror held up to the religious leaders of His day, Matthew 15:8-9. The occasion is a quarrel about hand washing, but His point is wider. A tradition passed down by teachers can end up occupying the place that belongs to the word of God, Mark 7:8-9. He is not condemning worship or inheritance as such, since He kept the feasts and read in the synagogue. He is applying Isaiah's test, whether the heart is near.

It leads to Christ by fulfilment of promise. The day described in verses 17 to 24 is one on which deaf ears hear the words of the scroll and blind eyes see. When John the Baptist asked if Jesus was the coming One, Jesus answered by pointing to what was happening, the blind seeing and the deaf hearing, Matthew 11:4-5. He was not offering evidence of the usual kind. He was saying that the long hoped for day of Isaiah had begun in Him. Jesus also notes that the humble and the poor are the ones to whom the good news comes, Matthew 11:5, which is the same pairing as verse 19. And He thanks the Father that what was hidden from the wise and learned has been revealed to little children, Matthew 11:25, a direct echo of verse 14 and of the humble in verse 19.

It leads to Christ by the Spirit of understanding. After His resurrection He opened the minds of His disciples to understand the Scriptures, Luke 24:45. This is the real removal of the seal. What no scholar could read, because the vision was closed, becomes intelligible in the one to whom it points. Revelation 5 makes the same claim in picture: He alone opens the scroll.

Paul sees the cross as the fulfilment of verse 14. God destroyed the wisdom of the wise by a message the world calls foolish, 1 Corinthians 1:18-21. The great irony is that the thing the wise could not accept was the wisdom of God, and the foolish things were the means of shaming the wise.

One caution keeps the reading honest. Isaiah is speaking to a historical Jerusalem under a historical siege. The chapter does not need to be turned into a code for Jesus, and the siege imagery of verses 1 to 8 is better left as a picture of the LORD's power than forced into a detailed pattern. The links that hold weight are the ones the New Testament itself makes: the quotation of verse 13, the use of verse 14 for the cross, verse 16 for God's right as Potter, and the signs of verse 18 as the work of the Messiah.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who can both besiege His own city and defend it. The one who says 'I will constrain Ariel' in verse 2 and 'I will camp in a circle around you' in verse 3 is the same LORD of Hosts who in verse 6 visits the attackers with thunder, earthquake and fire. The two actions do not conflict. Assyria is not an independent force that God merely allows. The chapter treats the siege as His instrument and the deliverance as His act, and it leaves no room for a story in which the nations decide Jerusalem's fate.

He is the God who sees. Verse 15 gives the foolish question, 'Who sees us, and who will know?' and the chapter answers it by the potter image. A maker knows what he has made. The plotters imagine that darkness is cover, but in Scripture darkness and light are alike to God, Psalm 139:11-12. The doctrine of God's knowledge is not a threat here so much as a fact that makes honest dealing possible.

He is the God who judges hollow worship, and who does so with great restraint. The chapter pictures Him responding to lip service with astonishment, 'wonder upon wonder,' and not with silence. Even His confounding of the wise is a kind of mercy, since it clears away the confidence that blocks the way to learning. His judgment is not an end in itself. It makes room for the day when the humble 'increase their joy in the LORD.'

He is also the Redeemer of Abraham, verse 22. The reference reaches behind Israel's history to the call of a man from an idolatrous family, Joshua 24:2, and reminds the nation that its existence depends on God's grace and not on its merit. The same God who redeemed Abraham will see that Jacob is no longer ashamed. The children are 'the work of My hands,' verse 23, and they will 'sanctify the Holy One of Jacob,' so that holiness is both His character and the response He draws from His people.

There is a tension the chapter does not resolve and does not need to. God is sovereign over blindness and sight, and yet the people are responsible for their lips and their plots. Worship, then, is neither a performance to impress Him nor a formula to be repeated. It is the response of the humble who have been given ears. Hearing the words of the scroll is itself a gift, and the right posture before a God who gives sight is the one the chapter ends on: instruction accepted, awe, and joy.

crossReferences.note: The angel of the LORD strikes the Assyrian camp overnight, and Sennacherib withdraws. It is the best-known historical fit for the sudden end of the besieging host in Isaiah 29:5-8, with the dead found in the morning as the dreamer wakes to find nothing in his hands.

The psalmist says the wicked are like a dream when one wakes, and the LORD despises their form when He rises. It is the same picture as Isaiah 29:7-8, where the nations who besieged Ariel prove as insubstantial as the meal in a hungry man's dream.

Isaiah is told to bind up the testimony and seal the law among his disciples. The sealed word is thus part of Isaiah's own ministry, and Isaiah 29:11-12 shows what happens when a nation will not receive it: the vision becomes a scroll that no one can open.

Jesus quotes the Greek form of Isaiah 29:13 against Pharisees and scribes who put tradition in the place of God's commandment. It shows that He read the chapter as a diagnosis that was still true of religious leaders who kept the forms while the heart stayed far away.

Paul draws on the potter and clay language of Isaiah 29:16 when he answers the objection that God has no right to find fault. The footnote in the BSB marks the citation. The point in both passages is that the clay cannot instruct the potter.

Paul cites Isaiah 29:14 to explain the cross: God destroys the wisdom of the wise and sets aside the intelligence of the intelligent. The same God who confounded Jerusalem's counsellors has now chosen to save through what the world calls foolish.

Paul quotes a combination of Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10 to say that God gave a spirit of stupor to many in Israel. It shows how Isaiah's deep sleep is taken up as part of the explanation for Israel's unbelief, which Paul insists is neither total nor final.

Nearly the same words as Isaiah 29:17 appear here, the orchard seeming like a forest, but now the change comes when the Spirit is poured out from on high. The echo suggests that the transformation promised in chapter 29 is the work of the Spirit.

A scroll sealed with seven seals can be opened by none in heaven or on earth until the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, is found worthy. The image reaches back to the sealed vision of Isaiah 29:11 and answers the question of who can break the seal.

When John the Baptist asks whether Jesus is the one who is to come, Jesus tells him to report what they hear and see: the blind receive sight, the deaf hear, the poor have good news brought to them. These are the signs of Isaiah 29:18-19, now being fulfilled.

The LORD sets out to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem. Some readers see in this the larger horizon of the dream-like fading of the nations in Isaiah 29:7-8, a deliverance of the city that will not be limited to one Assyrian army.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning, God's people have been given His word and told to live by it, and from the beginning there has been a difference between hearing and receiving. In the garden the serpent's first move was a question about what God had said, Genesis 3:1. At Sinai the people promised obedience, Exodus 24:3, and the history of the nation that followed shows how often it was promised and not done. Isaiah 29 sits in this long story as an exact diagnosis. The people have the forms, the feasts, the prophets and the scroll, and still they cannot read. The trouble lies in the heart.

The chapter also sets up what the rest of the Bible will say about the way out. The sealed vision of verses 11 and 12 will be opened. The deaf will hear the words of the scroll. The humble will have joy. That is not a return to the old arrangement but something new: God Himself teaches, and the learned are put to shame by it. Jeremiah promises that God will write His law on hearts so that none will need to teach a neighbour to know the LORD, Jeremiah 31:33-34. Ezekiel promises that God will take out a heart of stone, Ezekiel 36:26. Isaiah 32:15 says that the Spirit will be poured out from on high.

The story comes to rest in Christ. He applies Isaiah's diagnosis to the leaders of His own day and then gives the cure. His healings are the sign that the day of Isaiah 29:18 has come, and His resurrection opens the minds of the disciples to the Scriptures, Luke 24:45. At Pentecost the Spirit is poured out and the word is heard in the languages of all the nations, Acts 2:4-11. It is the reversal of the deep sleep.

In the new creation the scroll is open. Revelation 5 shows the Lamb taking the sealed scroll and breaking the seals, and the whole creation sings. The humble who increased their joy in the LORD are gathered into a people from every nation, Revelation 7:9-10, and the God who redeemed Abraham sees His children around Him, the work of His hands, honoring His name. Ariel, the hearth of judgment, becomes at the end the city where there is no temple because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22.

quiz.q: What ultimately happens to the many nations besieging Ariel, according to verses 5 to 8?

options.text: They vanish suddenly, like a dream from which someone wakes still hungry and thirsty.
options.note: Verses 7 to 8 describe exactly this sudden, dreamlike vanishing of the attacking nations.

options.text: They successfully conquer and permanently occupy Jerusalem.
options.note: The opposite; the nations' attack comes to nothing, like a vanished dream.

options.text: They negotiate a peaceful surrender with favorable terms.
options.note: No negotiation is described; the deliverance is sudden and dramatic, not a negotiated peace.

options.text: They retreat slowly over the course of several decades.
options.note: The text emphasizes suddenness, in an instant, not a slow, decades-long retreat.

quiz.q: What does the LORD say is the real problem with the people's worship in verse 13?

options.text: They honor Him with their lips, but their hearts are far from Him.
options.note: This is the exact diagnosis given, and it is later quoted directly by Jesus in Matthew 15:8-9.

options.text: They have stopped performing religious rituals altogether.
options.note: The opposite; they continue outward ritual and lip service, which is precisely the problem exposed.

options.text: They worship too many different gods at once.
options.note: Not the specific charge in this verse; the issue is insincerity in worship of the LORD, not polytheism per se.

options.text: They have replaced the temple with private home worship.
options.note: Not addressed in this verse; the issue named is hearts far from God despite outward worship, not the location of worship.

quiz.q: What analogy does verse 16 use to describe those who hide their plans from the LORD?

options.text: They act as if the potter could be regarded as mere clay, unable to know his own creation.
options.note: Verse 16 uses precisely this potter and clay analogy to expose their folly.

options.text: They act like sheep following a shepherd faithfully.
options.note: The opposite; the image used is one of foolish rebellion, not faithful following.

options.text: They act like builders constructing a strong tower.
options.note: Not the image used in this verse; the specific analogy is potter and clay.

options.text: They act like farmers planting seeds in good soil.
options.note: A different agricultural image appears elsewhere in Isaiah, but this specific verse uses the potter and clay analogy.

quiz.q: What reversal is promised in verse 18 for the deaf and the blind?

options.text: The deaf will hear the words of the scroll, and the blind will see out of deep darkness.
options.note: Verse 18 states this reversal explicitly, later fulfilled in Christ's healing ministry.

options.text: The deaf and blind will remain permanently unchanged.
options.note: The opposite; the verse promises a dramatic, hopeful reversal for them.

options.text: Only the wealthy deaf and blind will be healed.
options.note: No such economic restriction is mentioned in the text.

options.text: The deaf and blind will be exiled from the community.
options.note: The opposite of the text's promise, which is inclusion and restoration, not exile.

quiz.q: How does Jesus directly connect Himself to this chapter's themes?

options.text: He quotes verse 13 against hollow worship and fulfills verse 18 by healing the deaf and blind.
options.note: Matthew 15:8-9 quotes verse 13 directly, and Matthew 11:4-5 cites the healing of the deaf and blind as messianic proof.

options.text: He never references this chapter in any of the Gospels.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus directly quotes this chapter and fulfills its healing promise.

options.text: He only references it once in a minor, disputed parable.
options.note: The connection is a direct, undisputed quotation and a clear fulfillment, not a minor or disputed reference.

options.text: He references it solely to condemn the Gentile nations.
options.note: Jesus applies this chapter's critique to Jewish religious leaders and fulfills its healing promise broadly, not as a condemnation aimed at Gentiles.

questions: Jerusalem's attackers vanished suddenly, like waking from a dream. What overwhelming threat in your own life needs you to trust that God can dissolve it just as suddenly and completely?
The people honored God with their lips while their hearts stayed far from Him. Where might your own worship or religious habits have become more performance than genuine devotion?
Those who hid their plans from the LORD forgot that the potter always knows His own clay. What are you currently trying to hide from God that He already fully sees?
The promised reversal is that the deaf will hear and the blind will see. Where do you need God to open your own ears or eyes to something you have been missing or refusing to see?
The humble are promised increasing joy in the LORD. What would it look like this week to actively choose humility in a specific relationship or situation, trusting that joy, not loss, follows it?

translationNotes.note: Ariel is a name for Jerusalem whose meaning is debated, most likely altar hearth, though lion of God is also proposed; the wordplay casts the city's coming siege as a strange kind of sacrificial ordeal.
The sealed scroll here describes a vision made unintelligible to its hearers, an image later dramatically reversed in Revelation 5, where Christ alone is found worthy to open a sealed scroll.
This verse is quoted by Jesus in Matthew 15:8-9 against the Pharisees, applying Isaiah's ancient critique of hollow worship directly to religious leaders of His own day.
